tldr: The headline layer presents the Manila Rubio-Lavrov encounter almost universally as a diplomacy-deadlock story — 'no quick deal,' 'new ideas needed,' 'no breakthroughs' — with a secondary security thread in Iran-focused and Southeast Asian outlets foregrounding the US-Iran war as the week's dominant shadow. The economic fallout of Hormuz closure, central to body-level reporting, is entirely absent from the headline layer.

single_outlet_findings.finding: The only outlet to make the media-vs-diplomacy conflict the headline story, framing Rubio's closed-door approach as professional discipline rather than a transparency concern.

The only outlet to use 'dead Anchorage plan' in a headline — an editorial verdict that the Alaska summit framework is defunct, distinct from other Russian outlets that report the meeting without evaluating its outcomes.

The only outlet to pair explicit threat language ('Pay a Very Heavy Price') with a policy label ('Head for an Eye') in the headline, framing US-Iran policy in retaliatory terms not seen elsewhere in the cluster.

The most explicitly pessimistic headline in the cluster — 'No Breakthroughs, Little Optimism' — setting an unambiguously negative tone that other outlets, even those reporting the same absence of progress, avoided in their titles.

bottom_line: Headlines across the cluster sell the Manila meeting as managed stalemate — 'no quick deal,' 'new ideas needed,' 'no breakthroughs' — while Iran-focused and African outlets use their titles to foreground active war, revealing a gap between how Ukraine diplomacy and US-Iran escalation are packaged at the reader's first point of contact.
